introduction-the-microservice-detective.core: A single user request may cross a gateway, ten services, queues and databases. When it's slow or fails, metrics show something is wrong and logs show fragments, but neither shows the path. Distributed tracing records the request's journey as a tree of timed operations across services, so you can see exactly where time went and where errors originated.

first_principles.problem: Checkout takes 3 seconds, and five teams each insist their service is fast.
truths: Each service sees only its part.

analogy.title: A parcel tracking history
analogy.story: Every depot scans the parcel with time stamps, so you see exactly where it sat for two days.
analogy.breaks: Parcels follow one path; requests fan out in parallel.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Bottleneck is fraud-check, two hops deep.

check.q: What can tracing show that metrics and logs can't easily?
check.a: The causal path and timing of a single request across all services, revealing which hop is slow or failing.

the-building-blocks-spans-and-traces.core: A span represents one operation: a name, start and end time, status, attributes (http.route, db.system), events, and IDs: trace_id (shared by the whole request), span_id (unique) and parent_span_id (linking to its caller). A trace is the tree of spans sharing a trace_id. Span kinds (SERVER, CLIENT, PRODUCER, CONSUMER, INTERNAL) describe roles, and links connect related traces such as batch consumers.

first_principles.problem: An engineer instruments code but every service shows a separate one-span trace instead of one connected tree.

analogy.title: A family tree of tasks
analogy.story: The main task (root span) has children (sub-tasks), each with grandchildren, all sharing a family name (trace ID).
analogy.breaks: Families don't run in parallel; spans often do.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Child span under the current request with attributes and errors.

code.text:
from opentelemetry import trace
tracer = trace.get_tracer("checkout")

with tracer.start_as_current_span("reserve_inventory", kind=trace.SpanKind.INTERNAL) as span:
    span.set_attribute("cart.items", len(items))
    try:
        inventory.reserve(items)
    except Exception as e:
        span.record_exception(e)
        span.set_status(trace.Status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR))
        raise

check.q: What links a child span to its parent?
check.a: The parent_span_id field (with the shared trace_id), set from the active or propagated context.

context-propagation-connecting-the-dots.core: For spans in different services to join one trace, the trace context must travel with each request. The W3C traceparent header (version-traceid-parentid-flags) is injected by the caller's instrumentation and extracted by the callee, which creates child spans from it. Message queues carry it in message headers, and baggage carries extra key/values. Any hop that drops headers breaks the trace.

first_principles.problem: Traces stop at the API gateway because it doesn't forward the traceparent header to backends.

analogy.title: A relay baton
analogy.story: Each runner must hand the baton to the next; drop it and the race record breaks.
analogy.breaks: Batons are physical; headers can be stripped silently by middleware.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Callee continues the same trace as a child.

code.text:
GET /api/prices HTTP/1.1
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
#             ver|---------- trace-id ----------|-- parent-id --|flags(sampled)
baggage: tenant=acme,plan=pro

check.q: What does the last field (flags) in traceparent indicate?
check.a: Trace flags, notably the sampled bit telling downstream services whether this trace is being recorded.

opentelemetry-otel-the-industry-standard.core: OpenTelemetry is the CNCF standard for generating and exporting telemetry. It provides vendor-neutral APIs and SDKs in many languages, auto-instrumentation for common frameworks, the OTLP wire protocol, semantic conventions for attribute names, and the Collector to receive, process and export to any backend (Jaeger, Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb). Instrument once and switch vendors without touching code.

first_principles.problem: Switching from one APM vendor to another would require re-instrumenting 80 services.

analogy.title: A universal power socket standard
analogy.story: Appliances built to the standard work in any building, whichever electricity supplier you use.
analogy.breaks: Sockets are static; OTel semantic conventions evolve.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: HTTP, DB and client spans without code changes.

code.text:
pip install opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp
opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install
OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=checkout \
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317 \
opentelemetry-instrument python app.py

check.a: The OpenTelemetry Protocol, the standard wire format (gRPC/HTTP) for sending traces, metrics and logs to collectors and backends.

spans-vs-events.core: A span has duration and represents an operation; a span event is a timestamped point within a span ('cache miss', 'retry #2', an exception with stack trace). Use child spans for operations whose duration matters, and events for notable moments inside an operation. That avoids cluttering traces with thousands of tiny spans while still capturing what happened and when.

first_principles.problem: A trace has 3,000 child spans, one per loop iteration, making it unreadable and expensive.
truths: Too many spans add cost and noise.
derivation: Aggregate loops into **one span with counts**.

analogy.title: Chapters vs margin notes
analogy.story: Chapters (spans) structure the story; margin notes (events) mark notable moments without new chapters.
analogy.breaks: Books have no storage cost; spans do.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One span shows retries as events, not three spans.

check.q: When should you create a span rather than an event?
check.a: When the operation's duration matters and it may have its own children; use events for instantaneous moments.

sampling-strategies-handling-the-flood.core: Recording every trace at high traffic is costly. Head sampling decides at the start (keep 10% by trace ID ratio), which is cheap and consistent but blind to which traces turn out interesting. Tail sampling decides after the trace completes, keeping all errors, slow traces and a sample of the rest, which needs buffering in collectors. Parent-based sampling ensures downstream services follow the root's decision.

first_principles.problem: At 1% head sampling, the rare error traces the team needs are almost never captured.
truths: Decisions must be consistent across services.
derivation: Use **metrics** for exact rates (not sampled traces).

analogy.title: Choosing which flights to record in detail
analogy.story: Record a random 10% from the start, or wait until landing and keep every flight that had turbulence.
analogy.breaks: Flight recorders are cheap to buffer; tail sampling needs RAM for every in-flight trace.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: All errors and slow traces kept; 5% of the rest.

check.q: Why does tail sampling need more infrastructure than head sampling?
check.a: All spans of a trace must be buffered in one place until the trace completes before deciding, requiring memory and trace-aware routing.
